home.title: Code. Systems. Graphics.
home.intro: I’m Ali Raza, a developer and graphic designer based in Bolton, UK. I recently graduated from The Sixth Form Bolton, where I studied Computer Science, Graphics and ICT, and I now focus on building independent software and creative technology projects. My work spans AI systems, full-stack web development, Linux, automation and visual design. I enjoy taking complex ideas, understanding how they work from the inside out, and turning them into useful, distinctive experiences.
about: I’m most at home where technical problem-solving and visual thinking overlap. I like understanding systems from the inside out, finding the awkward parts, then designing better ways to solve them. Whether I’m building a local AI assistant, a personal operating system, a web application or a visual identity, I care about how the pieces work together rather than simply making something that works once.

My practice is self-directed and hands-on. I’ve built and deployed projects using Python, Flask, SQLite, JavaScript, HTML and CSS, while exploring technologies including LLMs, local AI, browser automation, vector databases, Linux desktop control and text-to-speech. Alongside software, my background in graphics gives me a strong interest in visual communication, interface design and making technical products feel intentional.

I’m particularly interested in building tools that give people more control over their technology. Projects such as CIEL, my local-first AI assistant, and LifeOS, my personal productivity and life-management platform, reflect that approach: understand the problem, build the system, test it in the real world, then keep improving it.
I speak English and Spanish fluently, with Urdu as my native language.

projects.title: CIEL
projects.subtitle: Central Intelligence & Execution Layer
projects.summary: A local-first AI assistant and execution layer designed to bridge natural-language interaction with real computer operations. CIEL combines conversational reasoning with persistent memory, system control, browser automation, web search, coding agents, scheduled tasks and local services.
details: I designed and developed CIEL as a modular personal computing assistant rather than a simple chatbot.

It combines conversational AI with real system capabilities including filesystem operations, shell commands, Arch Linux desktop control, web search through SearXNG, browser automation with Playwright, email access, scheduled tasks, LifeOS integration, text-to-speech and independent coding agents.
Its memory architecture combines ChromaDB for semantic retrieval with SQLite and structured fact storage so that different types of information can be retrieved appropriately.

I built the system around a routing and orchestration layer that determines how requests should be handled, with specialist workflows for coding, research, system design and code review, alongside ReAct-style execution loops, task queues and markdown-based skills.

One of the main challenges was preventing a system with many capabilities from becoming an unstructured collection of tools, so I separated reasoning, routing, memory and execution into distinct responsibilities and designed capabilities around defined interfaces and workflows.

This project taught me how complexity grows when AI models, tools and external systems are combined, and gave me practical experience in system architecture, agent orchestration, memory design, asynchronous execution, Linux automation and API integration.
ARIA was also explored as an experimental architecture during CIEL's development and is treated as part of CIEL rather than a separate project.

projects.title: LifeOS
projects.subtitle: Personal Operating System
projects.summary: A full-stack personal management platform designed to bring tasks, habits, projects, goals, journaling, notes, finance and personal planning into one system.
details: I designed and developed LifeOS as a central platform for managing different areas of personal life.
The application includes dashboards, tasks, habits, projects, goals, analytics, calendars, notes, journals, profiles and wider life-management modules.
I built both the backend and frontend and deployed the application for real-world use.
The backend is written in Python using Flask, with SQLite providing the database layer, while the frontend uses HTML, CSS and JavaScript with API endpoints connecting the interface to the backend.
The project also includes authentication, database-backed application logic, multiple API blueprints, bank-statement importing and integration with CIEL.
As the application grew from a simple personal tool into a larger platform, one of the main challenges was keeping the code maintainable as new features were added.
I learned to separate functionality into logical modules and API boundaries rather than continually expanding a single application layer.
I also had to diagnose and fix issues after deployment, which taught me to consider reliability and real-world behaviour rather than only whether code worked locally.
LifeOS gave me practical experience across the full development lifecycle, from database design and backend APIs through frontend development, debugging and deployment.

projects.title: ADML
projects.subtitle: AutoDesign Markup Language
projects.summary: A declarative design language and compiler pipeline that converts structured design instructions into outputs such as PowerPoint, SVG and live HTML previews.
details: I designed ADML as a custom markup language for describing visual designs using structured, human-readable instructions rather than manually specifying every pixel-level detail.
The project includes a language specification, parser and compiler pipeline, validation system and multiple output renderers.
ADML source is converted into an internal representation before being passed through format-specific rendering stages, allowing the same high-level design to be rendered as PowerPoint, SVG or HTML.

I also built command-line tooling for compiling, validating, previewing and inspecting supported formats, alongside documentation covering the language specification, abstract design types, rendering architecture and guidance for developers and AI systems generating ADML.
The main challenge was creating an abstraction expressive enough to describe complex layouts while remaining predictable for a compiler and easy for humans or AI systems to generate.
I approached this by separating design intent from the final output format, allowing the underlying representation to remain independent from individual renderers.

Through ADML I developed a deeper understanding of language design, parsing, intermediate representations, compiler architecture and abstraction, while also learning the importance of designing systems around clear specifications rather than allowing implementation details to define the architecture.

projects.title: PCP
projects.subtitle: Portable Compute Protocol
projects.summary: A systems project exploring how a complete personal computing environment could be carried on portable storage and run using the hardware of different host machines.
details: I designed PCP around the idea that a complete computing environment should be portable rather than tied to one physical computer.

The concept uses a portable Arch Linux environment containing the operating system, applications, configuration and user data, while the host machine provides hardware resources such as compute, display, networking and input/output.
The project explores bootable Arch environments, read-only operating system storage, encrypted persistent data, authentication, session state and interaction with host hardware.

The central challenge is that operating systems normally assume a fixed relationship between software and hardware, so I approached PCP by treating the host as a resource provider and the portable environment as the user's persistent computing layer.
This required me to think about boot processes, hardware compatibility, storage architecture, security and what information should persist between machines.

PCP strengthened my understanding of Linux internals, boot systems, storage, filesystem architecture, hardware abstraction and systems design, while teaching me to think about computing environments as collections of interacting layers rather than simply an operating system installed on a particular machine.

projects.title: DevTool
projects.subtitle: Local Developer Project Manager
projects.summary: A local command-line developer tool for managing software projects, development environments and common project workflows from a single interface.
details: I built DevTool to reduce the repetitive setup and management work involved in working across multiple local software projects.
It provides commands for creating and registering projects, navigating to projects, starting and running them, and managing their active, inactive and archived states.
It also includes environment-management functionality such as automated handling of Python virtual environments.
Rather than relying on a collection of shell aliases and manually maintained directories, DevTool provides a structured layer over the local development workspace.

I approached the project by identifying repetitive operations in my own development workflow and turning them into predictable commands, while keeping the underlying behaviour transparent and controllable.

This project taught me how useful focused developer tooling can be even when the underlying operations are relatively simple, and gave me experience designing CLI interfaces, managing local environments, structuring filesystem-based workflows and thinking about software from the perspective of another developer.

projects.title: Homelab Dashboard
projects.subtitle: lxServer Dashboard
projects.summary: A self-hosted web dashboard for monitoring and safely managing development projects running on a Linux homelab server.
details: I built a lightweight web interface for managing projects on my Linux homelab.

The dashboard discovers projects within a configured development directory, displays project information and system statistics, provides project logs and exposes a controlled set of management actions.
The backend uses FastAPI and Uvicorn, with SQLite for application data and session management, while the frontend uses standard HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
I implemented authentication using username and password credentials, bcrypt password hashing and server-side sessions.
System information is collected with psutil, while WebSockets provide live log streaming.
One of the main design considerations was giving a web interface useful control over a server without turning it into an unrestricted remote shell.
I therefore separated safe predefined operations from arbitrary command execution and designed the dashboard around explicit capabilities and allowlisted actions.

This project taught me about building internal infrastructure tools where security and operational reliability matter alongside functionality, giving me practical experience with FastAPI, WebSockets, authentication, system monitoring, process management and safer approaches to remote administration.

projects.title: Content Pipeline
projects.subtitle: Automated Faceless Content Production
projects.summary: An automated production pipeline for generating, processing, rendering and publishing short-form faceless video content.
details: I developed Content Pipeline as an end-to-end automation system for producing short-form video content.

Rather than treating video creation as a single script, I designed the process as a sequence of jobs covering story generation, voiceover processing, background media, captions, rendering and publishing.
Python coordinates the pipeline while FFmpeg and ffprobe handle media processing.

The system uses FIFO-style buffers for content components, a job state machine for tracking production stages, Whisper-based caption generation, external services for language and voice generation, configuration files and dry-run support.
Publishing workflows include platform-specific handling for services such as YouTube and TikTok.

The main challenge was making a multi-stage media process reliable enough to run repeatedly without manually supervising every step, so I approached each stage as a distinct job with explicit state, validation and failure boundaries.
This makes it possible to identify where a production run failed instead of treating the entire workflow as one opaque process.

The project taught me about pipeline architecture, media processing, automation reliability and designing systems around asynchronous and failure-prone operations, while reinforcing that reliable automation requires state management, validation, retries, configuration and clear failure handling rather than simply connecting APIs together.

graphicsProjects.title: Bliss55
graphicsProjects.overview: A multi-flavor brand identity and packaging system developed for the AQA ESA brief for Bliss55, a sparkling fruit drink line. The identity spans three flavor variants Cherry, Orange, and Apple Fizz combining flat vector illustration, bold logotype design, and promotional campaign assets to build a cohesive commercial identity aimed at a contemporary market.
brief: Design graphics for a brand of sparkling fruit drink named ‘Bliss55’.
thinking: Established a flexible visual system where each flavor variant retains core brand typography while adopting distinct color palettes and vector artwork motifs.
Explored flat, high-contrast vector styles to give the brand a modern, graphic look that scales cleanly across packaging and promotional media.
Used silhouette-driven illustrations (cherry blossom branches, palm trees, and profile vector art) to create immediate flavor recognition on shelf and in advertising.
process: Research & Ideation: Explored contemporary beverage design trends, focusing on minimal vector art and stylized fruit motifs to target a modern audience.
Vector Illustration & Layout: Created custom vector assets for each flavor, balancing organic lines with geometric shapes and bold typography.
3D Mockups: Rendered the flat graphics onto 3D drink can mockups to evaluate front-facing compositions, scale, and color hierarchy on curved surfaces.
Campaign Extension: Extended the visual identity into promotional campaign posters for each flavor, integrating display typography and contextual graphics.
outcome: A complete 9-piece design suite featuring 3 distinct flavor variants with 3D can renders, raw packaging layouts, and promotional posters.
A scalable brand system that demonstrates visual consistency across multi-product packaging and marketing collateral.

pieces.title: Cherry Can

pieces.description: Can mockup of the Bliss55 Cherry flavor packaging concept. The design features soft pink tones paired with vibrant red cherries and delicate vector cherry blossom branches, balancing organic botanical shapes with bold black logotype typography. Designed for high shelf impact, the layout uses sharp contrast and clean negative space to communicate a fresh, modern aesthetic.

pieces.title: Mockup Cherry Showcase
pieces.alt: Artwork from the Bliss55 graphic design collection, piece 02.
pieces.description: Flat visual presentation displaying the raw packaging artwork alongside the rendered Cherry can model. This layout highlights the spatial relationship between the background vector graphics, the floating 'CHERRY' flavor text, and the central product render, demonstrating how the packaging artwork translates from 2D vector art to a 3D product environment.

pieces.title: Orange Can
pieces.alt: Artwork from the Bliss55 graphic design collection, piece 03.

Utilizing a warm, tropical palette of muted terracotta, deep green, and soft coral, the design features a stylized palm tree silhouette paired with a geometric orange slice motif. The bold black 'BLISS' logotype and coral '55' branding maintain visual continuity across the product line.

pieces.title: Mockup Orange Showcase
pieces.alt: Artwork from the Bliss55 graphic design collection, piece 04.
pieces.description: Display layout for the Orange flavor variant, showing the rendered can centered against its underlying graphic elements. The composition emphasizes the curved wave lines, warm sun backdrop, and arched 'ORANGE' flavor typography, illustrating how individual graphic components build the variant's visual identity.

pieces.title: Apple Can
pieces.alt: Artwork from the Bliss55 graphic design collection, piece 05.
pieces.description: Can packaging render for the Bliss55 Apple Fizz variant. Featuring a crisp, cream-colored base with floating bubble vectors, the design incorporates a stylized vector profile integrated into a green apple silhouette. The lime green '55' branding and bold 'Apple Fizz' typography create a vibrant, refreshing aesthetic tailored to the flavor profile.

pieces.title: Mockup Apple Showcase

pieces.description: Flat presentation of the Apple Fizz design concept, positioning the 3D can render beside a large-scale vector illustration of the female profile motif. pieces.title: Bliss55 | Apple Poster

The composition frames the central product render with dynamic, rising bubble vectors, an enlarged green apple illustration, and bold display typography along the bottom margin. The design uses vertical hierarchy and high-contrast vector elements to create an energetic advertising asset.

pieces.title: Bliss55 | Cherry Poster

The artwork uses layered cherry blossom branches and falling petal vectors framed within a soft circular backdrop, creating a focused, seasonal poster design that reinforces the brand's botanical themes.

The poster demonstrates how the brand identity extends into vibrant commercial marketing assets.
